description.en: From the Nazi rise to power to Hiroshima: the key turning points of the most destructive war in history, in Europe, on the Eastern Front and in the Pacific.

text.en: On 30 January 1933 President Hindenburg appointed the Nazi leader Adolf Hitler Chancellor of Germany. Within months the Nazis banned other parties and set up a dictatorship that led to the Second World War and the Holocaust.

A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing in July 1937 escalated into full-scale war between Japan and China. Marked by atrocities such as the Nanjing Massacre, it killed millions and from 1941 merged into the Second World War.

In September 1938 Chamberlain and Daladier agreed to give Germany Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland without the Czechoslovaks at the table. Six months later Hitler occupied the whole country, and appeasement had failed.

On 23 August 1939 the USSR and Germany signed a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe into spheres of influence. Germany invaded Poland on 1 September; Soviet troops entered its eastern regions on 17 September.
On 1 September 1939 Germany invaded Poland. The war between the Axis and the Allies engulfed much of the world and killed tens of millions, including the victims of the Holocaust.
On 22 June 1941 Germany and its allies invaded the Soviet Union, beginning what Russians call the Great Patriotic War. The Brest Fortress garrison held out for weeks.
From 8 September 1941 to 27 January 1944 German and Finnish forces besieged Leningrad for 872 days. Estimates of deaths from hunger, cold and shelling range from 600,000 to 1.5 million.

In 1941–1945 Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murdered the Jews of Europe: in mass shootings in the occupied Soviet territories, in ghettos and in the death camps of Auschwitz, Treblinka and Sobibor. Around six million Jews were killed, along with hundreds of thousands of Roma, Soviet prisoners of war, disabled people and other victims of Nazi extermination policy.

On 7 December 1941 Japanese aircraft launched a surprise attack on the main base of the US Pacific Fleet in Hawaii, killing about 2,400 Americans. The next day the United States declared war on Japan and entered the Second World War.
From July 1942 to February 1943 the armies fought for Stalingrad on the Volga. The Soviet counteroffensive, Operation Uranus, encircled Paulus's Sixth Army, which surrendered on 2 February 1943.

On 5 July 1943 the Wehrmacht attacked the Kursk salient in Operation Citadel but was halted, with a major tank battle at Prokhorovka on 12 July. Afterwards the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Red Army.

On 6 June 1944 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on the Normandy coast in the largest seaborne invasion in history. The Second Front in Europe was opened, and the liberation of France soon followed.

After Soviet troops took Berlin, Germany's unconditional surrender was signed at Karlshorst late on 8 May 1945, already 9 May in Moscow. The date became Victory Day in the USSR, marking the end of the war against Germany.
On 6 August 1945 a US bomber dropped an atomic bomb on Hiroshima, and on 9 August another on Nagasaki. Well over 100,000 people died, many later from radiation sickness.
